content: The use of conventional cardiotocography (CTG) for monitoring fetal well-being during labor has been associated with an increased rate of cesarean sections compared to intermittent auscultation of the fetal heart rate. However, this approach has been shown to reduce the incidence of neonatal seizures, although it does not significantly affect other neonatal outcomes. To improve the sensitivity of fetal monitoring and reduce the number of cesarean sections performed for nonreassuring fetal status, additional methods of fetal assessment have been explored. For instance, fetal scalp blood sampling for pH or lactate measurement has demonstrated some efficacy in reducing cesarean section rates. The adaptation of pulse oximetry for use in the fetus during labor has been proposed as a potential method to enhance fetal evaluation. This technique could theoretically reduce cesarean sections performed for nonreassuring fetal status without altering neonatal outcomes. The objective of this review was to compare the effectiveness and safety of fetal intrapartum pulse oximetry with other fetal surveillance techniques. The search strategy included the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of May 31, 2014), consultation with experts in the field, and examination of reference lists from retrieved studies. Previous searches of databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, and Current Contents were discontinued for this update, as they had not identified any additional trials beyond those already included in the Cochrane register. The review included all published and unpublished randomized controlled trials that compared maternal and fetal outcomes when fetal pulse oximetry was used during labor. This included comparisons of fetal pulse oximetry with or without concurrent use of CTG versus CTG alone, as well as comparisons of fetal pulse oximetry plus CTG with other methods such as fetal electrocardiography (ECG) plus CTG. Data extraction was performed independently by at least two review authors, and additional information was sought from the investigators of three trials. Seven trials were included in the review, six of which compared fetal pulse oximetry plus CTG with CTG alone (or with blinded fetal pulse oximetry values), and one trial compared fetal pulse oximetry plus CTG with fetal ECG plus CTG. These trials involved a total of 8013 pregnancies. However, the trials were at high risk of bias due to the impracticality of blinding participants and clinicians, as well as high or unclear risk of bias for outcome assessors in all but one report. Other sources of bias, such as selection bias, attrition bias, and reporting bias, were generally of low or unclear risk. The trials had differing entry criteria, which necessitated separate analyses rather than a meta-analysis of all trials. A systematic review of four trials involving pregnancies from 34 weeks' gestation that did not require fetal blood sampling prior to study entry found no evidence of differences in overall cesarean section rates between groups monitored with fetal pulse oximetry and those not monitored with fetal pulse oximetry or with masked pulse oximetry results (average risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.86 to 1.13, n = 4008, I² = 45%). One study reported a higher risk of cesarean section in the group monitored with fetal pulse oximetry plus CTG compared to the group monitored with fetal ECG plus CTG (n = 180, RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.29). Neonatal seizures and neonatal encephalopathy were rare in both groups, and no studies reported on long-term disability outcomes. There was evidence of a reduction in cesarean sections for nonreassuring fetal status in the fetal pulse oximetry plus CTG group compared to the CTG group in pregnancies from 34 weeks' gestation (average RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.90, n = 4008, I² = 63%). However, there was no evidence of differences between groups in cesarean sections performed for dystocia, although the overall incidence rates varied between trials. In conclusion, the addition of fetal pulse oximetry does not reduce overall cesarean section rates. One study found a higher cesarean section rate in the group monitored with fetal pulse oximetry plus CTG compared to the group monitored with fetal ECG plus CTG. The data provide limited support for the use of fetal pulse oximetry in the presence of a nonreassuring CTG to reduce cesarean sections for nonreassuring fetal status. A more effective method than pulse oximetry is needed to improve the overall evaluation of fetal well-being during labor.
